summary: What happened to a record, in order — an audit log, a record's history, a ticket's activity. An ordered list of TimelineItems, each one sentence: what happened, who did it, and when, in a real `<time>`. History only: every event is done, so there is no status and nothing is announced.
useWhen: a record's history — who changed what, and when
an audit log a person reads to find out what happened, newest first

useInstead.when: the steps of an agent run
useInstead.why: it has a status per step and announces the one in progress; a Timeline is history and says nothing on its own

useInstead.when: things the user has to read or act on — mentions, approvals, alerts
useInstead.why: it tracks read and unread and marks them; a Timeline is a record, not an inbox

useInstead.when: events the user sorts, filters or selects
useInstead.why: a log searched by column, exported or acted on in bulk is a table of events, not a story

useInstead.when: the entries are turns in a conversation — what a person asked and what an assistant answered
useInstead.why: a transcript is turns people took, each named by who and when; a Timeline is changes to a record

composition.note: Name the list with `aria-label` — or `aria-labelledby` pointing at the card or section heading above it. Order the items as they are read, usually newest first. Each item's `title` is what happened, as a sentence; `actor` is who; `timestamp` is when; children are the detail — what it changed from and to. For a long history, show the latest and put a "Show older" Button below the list.
composition.example: <Timeline aria-label="History"><TimelineItem title="Paused the agent" actor="Ada Reyes" timestamp={event.at} /></Timeline>

requires: `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby` — the list's name, the history of what
a `title` that says what happened in words — the icon and the line are not read
guarantees: it is an `<ol>`: a screen reader says how many events there are and which one it is on
each event reads in one order — what happened, who, when — then its detail
the time is a `<time>` with the exact instant in `dateTime`, whatever its label says
the line, the markers and any icon are hidden from assistive tech
it renders on a server: no hooks, no effects
notes: pass `locale` and `timeZone` to each item when rendering on a server, or its default label can differ from the browser's

antiPatterns.why: a column of divs is not a list: a screen reader cannot say how many events there are or skip past them

antiPatterns.dont: a green dot for "Approved" and a red one for "Rejected", with the title "Status changed"
antiPatterns.do: the title "Approved the refund" or "Rejected the refund"
antiPatterns.why: the dots are hidden from assistive tech and fail WCAG 1.4.1 for everyone else; what happened belongs in the words
the relative label keeps the exact instant in `dateTime`, which a bare span throws away
